title: Severe bleeding from an arm or leg
asks: how do I stop severe bleeding from a leg
arm is spurting blood what do i do
how to put on a tourniquet
bleeding wont stop from his arm
no tourniquet how do i stop the bleeding
how long can a tourniquet stay on
deep cut on thigh lots of blood help
chainsaw cut to the leg bleeding heavy
man down, gunshot to leg, heavy bleeding, what do i do, over
answer: Act now: severe bleeding can cause death in as little as 3 minutes.
Call for help immediately and plan evacuation to medical care.
Cut or tear clothing away to expose the whole wound.
Press hard directly on the source of the bleeding. Keep pressing until a tourniquet or dressing is in place.

Bleeding is life-threatening when: blood is pulsing or flowing steadily from the wound; clothes are soaked with blood; blood is pooling on the ground; an arm or leg has been cut or torn off; bandages keep soaking through with blood; or the person bled earlier and is now in shock (unconscious, confused and pale).
Life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg and you have a tourniquet: apply it immediately, 2 to 3 inches above the wound, directly on the skin, not over clothing.
Under fire, or when the source of the bleeding is unclear: put the tourniquet "high and tight" on the limb (under fire, over clothing) and move to cover. Re-check it once you are in a safer position.

Sources differ on when to use a tourniquet. Army first aid manual: immediately, for life-threatening bleeding from a limb. WHO: only if all other bleeding control has failed and the bleeding is life-threatening. HHS ship's medical manual: as the last resort, if serious bleeding cannot be stopped or a limb has been lost.
Tighten the tourniquet until the bleeding stops and no pulse can be felt below it, then lock it in place. Expect pain: it is a sign the tourniquet is applied properly.
If the bleeding does not stop, apply a second tourniquet next to the first, higher on the limb.
Write the exact time the tourniquet was applied on the person's skin or on the tourniquet itself.
No tourniquet: first pack the wound tightly with gauze or clean, dry cloth, directly over the heaviest bleeding, and hold firm, continuous direct pressure for at least 3 minutes.
If blood soaks through, do not remove the first dressing. Add more gauze and keep up firm pressure.
Once the bleeding is controlled, apply a pressure bandage over the packing to hold it in place. With no pressure bandage, keep up firm, direct pressure until medical help arrives.

Only if packing and pressure fail to control bleeding in an arm or leg, and as an absolute last resort, improvise a tourniquet: fold cloth to about 1 ½ to 2 inches wide, tighten it by twisting with a straight rod, then secure the rod so it does not loosen. Keep checking it: improvised tourniquets tend to loosen.

Keep the person warm, even in warm weather: keep them dry and off the ground, and cover them with blankets, sleeping bags or anything that holds heat. Blood loss causes hypothermia, and cold stops blood from clotting properly.
Keep re-checking the tourniquet and dressings to make sure they are still tight and working.
warnings: A tourniquet cuts off the blood supply to the limb. Use one only for life-threatening bleeding, not for minor bleeding.

Sources differ on loosening a tourniquet. The Army first aid manual says it should never be removed except by medical personnel, and the HHS ship's medical manual says to keep it tight until a physician orders it loosened. WHO says to release it every 2 hours for at least 10 minutes while holding direct pressure on the wound, and to re-apply it only if bleeding continues.
Tourniquet time: under 2 hours is safest. After that tissue may start to die, and the limb may be lost after 6 hours.
Do not place a tourniquet over a joint (knee or elbow), over the wound or over a fracture.
An improvised tourniquet that is too narrow may damage the skin. WHO: use a thick, wide band (the wider, the better).
If an object is stuck in the wound, do not remove it. Bandage it in place.
If the skin below a pressure bandage becomes cool, bluish or numb, the bandage may be too tight: loosen it and reapply.

quotes.text: The urgency of promptly stopping massive external bleeding cannot be overstated, as the longer a Service member bleeds from a major wound, the lower their chances of survival become. Severe injuries have the potential to cause death in as little as three minutes due to blood loss.

Use this technique ONLY if all other bleeding control measures have failed AND haemorrhage is life-threatening. If you place a tourniquet, there is a possibility that tissues below the tourniquet will be permanently damaged and even require amputation. If you are considering using a tourniquet, CALL FOR HELP IMMEDIATELY and plan for handover/transfer to a unit where surgery is possible.
Then, twist the stick until the bleeding stops, securing the stick to prevent unwinding. Note the date and time applied. EVACUATE THE PATIENT TO THE PHYSICIAN IMMEDIATELY.
During TFC, when evaluating the casualty for the location, type, and size of the wound or injury, it is essential to cut or tear their clothing and carefully expose the entire area of the wound.

Direct pressure can and should be used as a temporary measure until a TQ or dressing is in place. It is difficult to use direct pressure alone to control significant bleeding, or while moving the casualty.
Apply firm pressure as directly as possible to the source of bleeding, usually with two or three fingers.

Bleeding is considered life-threatening when— • There is pulsing or steady bleeding from the wound. • The overlying clothes are soaked with blood. • Blood is pooling on the ground. • There is a traumatic amputation of an extremity. • Bandages or makeshift bandages used to cover the wound are ineffective and are steadily becoming soaked with blood. • There was prior bleeding, and the patient is now in shock (unconscious, confused, and pale). 4-6. A TQ is immediately needed when any of the above examples are present on an extremity. Injury to a major vein or artery can result in shock or death from blood loss in minutes.

TQs serve as critical devices for halting severe bleeding from extremities, such as arms or legs, by effectively restricting blood flow when applied higher to the injury site, thus preventing further blood loss.
If the source of massive bleeding is evident, such as from an amputation or major wound, immediate bleeding control measures like applying a TQ or wound packing should be initiated
Although Tier 1 and Tier 2 provide the same hemorrhage control treatment of hasty TQ during CUF, during TFC the Tier 2 CLS treats any massive bleeding, from an extremity, with deliberate TQs.

A hasty TQ is implemented as "high and tight" on the wounded extremity or when the bleeding source is ambiguous during the CUF phase. However, during TFC, all TQs should be deliberate, placed two to three inches above the wound directly on the skin, not over clothing. Once the casualty is in a safer position, the bleeding source should be reassessed, and the effectiveness of the TQs verified.

Care under fire is the first phase of care in tactical combat casualty care where very limited care is provided for the casualty while the enemy threat is still active. Also known as CUF or care under threat.
Position the TQ above the bleeding site, high on the extremity over the clothing/uniform.
IF SERIOUS BLEEDING CANNOT BE STOPPED, or if the injury includes loss of a limb, apply a tourniquet, as the last resort.

Twist the rod until bleeding has stopped (complete steps 1-5 in under 1 min). • Lock the windlass rod in place with the windlass clip. • Route the self-adhering band around the rod and between the clips. • Secure the windlass safety strap. • If no other major bleeding is present, move to cover.
Apply enough pressure to make distal pulses disappear and re-assess bleeding.
Expecting pain during application is crucial as it signifies proper TQ application.
If bleeding persists despite a previously applied TQ, the CLS should promptly apply a second deliberate TQ adjacent to the original, positioned higher on the limb.
Record the exact time the tourniquet was applied in the notes AND write it on the patient’s skin or the tourniquet itself.

If a TQ is not available, pack the wound and hold direct pressure over the source of the heaviest bleed, FIRST. If this fails to control the bleeding in an arm or leg, only then consider an alternate improvised TQ.
If a hemostatic dressing is not available, use gauze or clean, dry cloth material. • Pack the hemostatic dressing tightly into the wound directly over the site that has the most active bleeding.
Fill and pack the whole wound cavity tightly while keeping firm pressure on the wound. More than one hemostatic dressing or gauze may be required to stop the blood flow.
After packing, continue to apply firm, manual pressure until the bleeding stops. Hold continuous direct pressure for a minimum of 3 minutes.
If the first dressing becomes soaked with blood, do not remove as this will dislodge any clots that have formed. Instead add another pad and apply firm pressure.
If the wound was previously packed with gauze or other materials, apply additional gauze or materials and pressure (for another 3 minutes) until bleeding has stopped.
Once bleeding has been controlled, apply a pressure bandage over the wound packing material to secure it in place.
In situations where pressure dressings are not available, maintaining firm, direct pressure is essential until medical assistance arrives.

In constructing one, it is recommended that you fold a cravat (or other pliable material) to a width of approximately 1 ½ to 2 inches and tighten it with some sort of windlass rod (a straight rod that can be used to twist the material tighter). Then secure the rod to ensure it does not loosen.
An improvised TQ should not be used except as an absolute last resort when there is no other option to control life-threatening bleeding.
Continue to check the TQ, as improvised TQs are prone to loosening due to (but not limited to) casualty movement, shifting fluid, and quality of improvised material.

Massive bleeding can cause hypothermia, which in turn can cause more bleeding because cold temperatures can prevent blood from clotting properly. This is a problem even in warm weather, and especially for people in shock who can’t generate enough body heat.

The first responder must prevent, and address hypothermia compounded by massive blood loss. This is not hypothermia due to cold weather, but can be prevented by— • Keeping clothing or uniform on the casualty. • Replacing extremely wet clothing if possible and keeping the casualty dry. • Keeping the casualty off the ground, by placing a barrier between the casualty and the ground or lifting them off the ground, if possible. Note. Contact with the ground increases loss of body heat. • Using dry blankets, poncho liners, sleeping bags, or anything that will retain heat. • Minimizing the casualty’s exposure to the environment.
Continuously reassess all bleeding control measures, such as tourniquets and pressure dressings, to ensure they remain effective and are adjusted tightly as soon as possible.
If you place a tourniquet, you are cutting off blood supply to the limb, so only do this for life-threatening bleeding.

It is crucial to recognize that TQs should be used cautiously, with the optimal safe duration being less than two hours. Beyond this timeframe, tissues may start to die, potentially leading to limb loss after six hours. Regular reassessment of TQ effectiveness is necessary, including checking for stopped bleeding, absent distal pulse, and ensuring no pulse below the TQ on the limb. Common errors when applying TQs include not using one, when necessary, not tightening it adequately, and using it for minimal bleeding. Additionally, TQs should never be removed except by medical personnel at a higher role of care.

Tourniquet use is dangerous and may cause unwanted loss of the limb. Keep the area uncovered and the tourniquet tight until ordered to be loosened by a physician. In general, if the bandaging was applied to control bleeding, do not remove. Seek medical care.

The tourniquet should be released every 2 hours for at least 10 minutes. Hold direct pressure to the bleeding area during this time. Do not re-apply the tourniquet unless evidence of continued active bleeding.
Care should be taken to avoid placing TQs over joints or pockets containing bulky items, ensuring the TQs effectiveness.
Do not put a TQ directly over the knee or elbow, over a holster, or cargo pocket that contains bulky items.
Apply as close to wound as possible, but do not place over a wound or a fracture.

The risks associated with using improvised TQs include: • Damage may occur to the skin if the band is too narrow. • Bleeding may worsen. • Bleeding may not be completely controlled. • Likely to loosen overtime from not being properly secured.
If not, use a thick band or piece of cloth or belt (the wider, the better), over padded skin.
If a penetrating object is lodged in the casualty’s body, bandage it in place. Do not remove the object.
If the skin below the pressure bandage becomes cool to touch, bluish, or numb, or if the distal pulse is no longer present, the pressure bandage may be too tight and should be loosened and reapplied.

conflict: Army ATP 4-02.11 (2026), WHO-ICRC Basic Emergency Care (2018) and HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003) disagree on tourniquets. (1) When: ATP 4-02.11 says 'A TQ is immediately needed' when any sign of life-threatening bleeding is present on a limb (an improvised one only as a last resort); WHO BEC says 'Use this technique ONLY if all other bleeding control measures have failed AND haemorrhage is life-threatening'; HHS says apply one 'as the last resort' if serious bleeding cannot be stopped or a limb is lost. (2) Loosening: ATP 4-02.11 says 'TQs should never be removed except by medical personnel at a higher role of care' and HHS says keep it tight 'until ordered to be loosened by a physician'; WHO BEC says 'The tourniquet should be released every 2 hours for at least 10 minutes', re-applying only if bleeding continues (WHO writes this for providers: 'You will not be expected to perform the tourniquet technique'). The card shows all positions for (1) and (2); the owner must choose. (3) Skin: ATP 4-02.11 places a deliberate tourniquet 'directly on the skin, not over clothing'; WHO BEC applies a blood pressure cuff or wide band 'over padded skin' (padding is not in the card). (4) WHO BEC also says to elevate a bleeding limb above the heart; ATP 4-02.11 does not mention elevation for massive bleeding (not in the card). (5) Soaked dressings: WHO BEC says never remove the first dressing; ATP 4-02.11 agrees for gauze (leave it, add more) but says an ineffective hemostatic dressing is removed and replaced when more are available; HHS says keep the first layer and replace the other soaked gauze. The card covers gauze or cloth only and says add more. (6) Pressure time: ATP 4-02.11 says hold direct pressure for a minimum of 3 minutes; HHS says 4-6 minutes. The card says at least 3 minutes. (7) 'High and tight when the source of the bleeding is unclear' rests on one ambiguous ATP 4-02.11 sentence (para 4-39) that ties hasty placement to care under fire. FEMA P-2064 (2020) was searched: it only advises taking a class on how to stop bleeding.
